procedural_history.originating_court: Metropolitan Magistrate-04 (N.I. Act)/South East, Saket Courts, New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 25.01.2019 by the Metropolitan Magistrate dismissing Criminal Complaints No.621744/16, 1718/16, 1276/ 16, 1277/16, 621743/16, 621742/16, 12742/17 and 12744/17 for non-appearance of the complainant (the appellant herein).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The complainant (appellant) challenged the Magistrate's order before the Delhi High Court through Crl.L.P. Nos.315 to 322 of 2019. The Delhi High Court dismissed these petitions via a common order dated 07.11.2019.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The complainant (appellant) filed special leave petitions before the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi High Court's order dated 07.11.2019. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the orders of the High Court and the Magistrate, and restored the proceedings to their original number(s) on the file of the learned Magistrate.

directions: The order(s) of the High Court as well as of the learned Magistrate are set-aside.

The proceedings shall stand restored to their original number(s) on the file of the learned Magistrate and the prosecution shall now proceed from the stage where it was when the order of acquittal/dismissal of the complaint(s) was passed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate was justified in dismissing the criminal complaints for non-appearance of the complainant, even though the complainant's evidence had already been recorded and the matter was posted for defence evidence.

facts: The complainant had filed criminal complaints against the accused.
The complainant's statement had been recorded, and they had been cross-examined.
The complainant's evidence was officially closed, and the case was scheduled for the recording of defence evidence.
The complainant had also filed an application under Section 311 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
On a subsequent date, the complainant failed to appear in court.
As a result, the Magistrate dismissed the complaints for non-appearance and acquitted the accused.
law: The case revolves around Section 256(1) of the CrPC, which generally requires a Magistrate to acquit an accused if the complainant does not appear on a scheduled hearing date.

However, the proviso to Section 256(1) gives the Magistrate discretion to dispense with the complainant's attendance and proceed with the case if their personal attendance is not considered necessary.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate acted incorrectly by dismissing the complaints outright.

The Court reasoned that since the complainant's evidence, including their examination and cross-examination, was already on the record, there was admissible evidence available for the court to consider.

This was a classic situation where the proviso to Section 256(1) CrPC should have been applied. The Magistrate could have determined that the complainant's personal presence was not necessary to proceed and could have decided the case on its merits based on the existing evidence.

Regarding the pending application under Section 311, the Court stated that if the complainant did not appear to argue it, the Magistrate could have simply rejected that application and continued with the main case, rather than dismissing the entire complaint.
The Court held that both the Magistrate and the High Court failed to consider that evidence was already on record, making the dismissal for non-appearance unjustified.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Magistrate was not justified in dismissing the complaints. It held that the lower courts should have proceeded with the case on its merits using the available evidence, as permitted by the proviso to Section 256(1) of the CrPC. Consequently, the Court set aside the orders of the Magistrate and the High Court and restored the complaints to the stage they were at before the dismissal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate was justified in dismissing the criminal complaints for non-appearance of the complainant, even though the complainant's evidence had already been recorded and the matter was posted for defence evidence.
appellant_arguments: The Magistrate failed to consider the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 256 of the Code, which allows the court to proceed with a case even in the complainant's absence if there is evidence on record.
Since the complainant's statement had been recorded and they had been cross-examined, there was admissible evidence on record, enabling the Magistrate to decide the case on its merits.
The complainant's non-appearance was due to being misled by their counsel into believing their presence was not required as a settlement was being negotiated.
Instead of dismissing the entire complaint, the Magistrate could have simply rejected the pending application under Section 311 and proceeded with the case based on the available evidence.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain the arguments made by the respondent.

cases.case_name: Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. Keshvanand
cases.principle: To discuss the purpose of inserting a provision like Section 256 of the Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 256 of the Code, where there is admissible evidence on record, such as the complainant's recorded statement and cross-examination, the Magistrate can proceed to decide the case on its merits even in the subsequent absence of the complainant.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that where the complainant's evidence has already been recorded, it is inappropriate for a Magistrate to dismiss the complaint and acquit the accused solely due to the complainant's non-appearance. The Magistrate had the alternative to reject any pending applications and proceed to decide the case on its merits based on the available evidence, making the dismissal an unjustified and disproportionate action.
legal_tests_applied: Where the complainant had already been examined as a witness in the case, it would not be appropriate for the Court to pass an order of acquittal merely on non- appearance of the complainant.
policy_considerations: The purpose of Section 256 of the Code is to afford protection to an accused against harassing tactics of a complainant. However, this does not mean that if the complainant is absent, the court has a mandatory duty to acquit the accused, especially when the case can be decided on its merits based on evidence already on record.
